papers.title_in_file: Efficient Reservoir Computing using Field Programmable Gate Array and Electro-optic Modulation
papers.version_note: arXiv v1 (2102.09049v1, 11 Feb 2021) text layer; equations are garbled in the text layer.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental opto-electronic reservoir computer (EOM plus FPGA) benchmarked on NARMA-10, Santa Fe laser prediction and spoken digit recognition.

assertions.value: The authors state they experimentally demonstrate a fully-packaged opto-electronic reservoir computing system consisting of a Mach-Zehnder electro-optic modulator (EOM) and an FPGA circuit.
quotes: experimentally demonstrate a fully-packaged opto-electronic RC system consisting of a Mach-Zehnder electro-optic modulator (EOM) and a FPGA circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states the system the paper builds.

assertions.value: The authors state that both the delay line and the filters are implemented digitally within the FPGA, and claim this renders the system compact and immune to optical drifts and noise compared with fiber-optical realizations.
quotes: both the delay line and ﬁlters are implemented digitally within FPGA
immune to optical drifts and noise, especially compared to ﬁber-optical realizations
assertions.certainty_reason: The immunity claim is an author claim with no direct test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper also uses a calibration DAC to compensate EOM bias drift (Section 3), so drift is not fully absent from the system.

assertions.value: The authors describe time-delay based reservoir computing as using virtual nodes that are temporally spaced, with only one nonlinear node, the nonlinearity being implemented electro-optically with an EOM.
quotes: the time-delay based RC uses virtual nodes that are temporally spaced and has only one nonlinear node
The non-linearity is implemented electro-optically, using an EOM.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the time-delay architecture the paper uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike other recurrent neural networks that they describe as notoriously hard to train, in reservoir computing only the output weights need to be optimized, which makes training much simpler.
quotes: Unlike other kinds of recurrent neural networks that are notoriously hard to be trained, here only the output weights are needed to be optimized, making the training much simpler.
assertions.certainty_reason: General statement about reservoir computing, no evidence given in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the first reservoir computing system was implemented using analog electronics with a single nonlinear node and delayed feedback, citing reference 17.
quotes: The ﬁrst RC system was implemented using analog electronics with a single nonlinear node and delayed feedback [17].
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the states are coupled using the filter coefficients and that the digital filter gives flexibility to implement different network topologies, citing reference 42.
quotes: the states are coupled using ﬁlter coeﬃcients
Digital ﬁlter gives the ﬂexibility to implement diﬀerent network topology [42].
assertions.certainty_reason: Statement of design property; no topology comparison is run in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment in the paper varies the filter to change the topology; every benchmark uses one filter design.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optical power at the EOM output is given by a transfer function of sine-squared form in the applied RF signal, the pi-shift voltage and a bias offset and that the detector, filter and delay give a discretized state equation.
quotes: The optical power at the output of EOM is given by a transfer function
The photo-detector generates voltage in response to the applied laser power which is given by
The ﬁltered data implements the Eq. (9) which has state information.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 2 defines the model the results depend on; equations are garbled in the text layer so only the prose is quoted.

assertions.value: The authors report a fiber-coupled laser diode giving a continuous wave beam near 1550 nm into an EOM, a photodetector digitized by an ADC with 1 Msps sampling rate controlled by the FPGA, and 16-bit ADC and RF DAC interfaced to the FPGA by Serial Peripheral Interface.
quotes: provides a continuous wave beam at ∼1550 nm
digitized using an analog to digital converter (ADC) with 1 Msps sampling rate controlled by FPGA
ADC (Maxim Integrated MAX11198, 16bits)
RF DAC (Analog Devices D5541A,16bits) using Serial Peripheral Interface
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 describes the hardware the results come from.

assertions.value: The authors report that the FPGA logic runs on a Zedboard (Zynq-7000) development platform with the reservoir logic written in Verilog, and that a PC supplies preprocessed data (mask and input scaling) over Ethernet and receives the state data back from the Processing System.
quotes: the FPGA blocks implemented on a Zedboard (Zynq-7000) development platform
The RC logic is implemented using Verilog programming language.
mask and input scaling factor, which is then sent to a Zedboard via Ethernet interface
PS will then transmit this data to PC via Ethernet interface.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the platform.

assertions.value: The authors report that the programmable delay block is limited to 1000 units, each delay representing one virtual node spacing, and that the finite digital bandpass filter has 400 filter taps.
quotes: programmable delay block with delay limited to 1000 units, each delay representing 1 virtual node spacing
ﬁnite digital bandpass ﬁlter which has 400 ﬁlter taps
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the hardware limits.
assertions.reader_inference: The Santa Fe headline result uses 950 nodes (Table 2) while the filter has 400 taps; the paper does not say how 950 nodes relates to the 400-tap filter.

assertions.value: The authors state that the programmable gain and offset are key parameters for tuning the performance of the reservoir computing system, and that a calibration DAC (16 bits) compensates the bias drift of the EOM.
quotes: Here, the gain and oﬀset are key parameters for tuning RC system performance.
Calibration DAC (Maxim Integrated MAX5316, 16bits) is used to compensate for the bias drift of EOM.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the tuning parameters and drift compensation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the NARMA10 input is drawn from a uniform distribution in the interval [0, 0.5], that performance is measured by the normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) between target and prediction, normalized by the standard deviation of the target.
quotes: is drawn from a uniform distribution in the interval [0, 0.5]
normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE) between the target and predicted value is calculated as
denotes the standard deviation of the target.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.1 defines the task and the metric.

assertions.value: The authors report NARMA10 results with 400 nodes: a mean NRMSE of 0.142 for 2000 samples and 0.148 for 25000 samples, with standard deviations 6.47 x 10^-3 and 5.90 x 10^-3 and minima 0.129 and 0.139 respectively (Table 1).
quotes: Table 1. NARMA10 benchmark results with 400 nodes.
Samples 2000 25000
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experimental system.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says predictions of 1000 and 25,000 steps give 0.142 and 0.148, while Table 1 labels the 0.142 column 2000 samples and Table 4 lists training/testing size 1000/1000; the sample count behind 0.142 is stated inconsistently.

assertions.value: The authors state that for 25000 samples with a training size of 5200 the mean NRMSE is 0.148, and they describe the system as performing well over long-term prediction.
quotes: For 25000 samples with training size of 5200, the mean NRMSE is 0.148.
the present RC performs remarkably well over long term prediction
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experimental system.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Santa Fe task uses data set A from the 1994 Santa Fe Institute competition, a time series measured from an NH3 laser, with one step prediction on 4000 data points, scored by NMSE.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.2, Santa Fe laser data prediction, p.6
quotes: The data set A from the 1994 time series prediction competition organized by the Santa Fe Institute
obtained from measuring a NH3 laser
Santa Fe laser data prediction is one step series prediction and we use 4000 data points in our test case.
The performance is measured using NMSE.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.2 states the task setup.

assertions.value: The authors report Santa Fe single step results (Table 2): with 400 nodes a mean NMSE of 2.71 x 10^-2 (std 6.20 x 10^-4, min 2.54 x 10^-2), and with 950 nodes a mean NMSE of 6.73 x 10^-3 (std 3.34 x 10^-4, min 5.66 x 10^-3).
quotes: Table 2. Santa Fe laser data single step benchmark results.
Nodes# 400 950
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experimental system.
assertions.reader_inference: The headline NMSE of 6.73 x 10^-3 in the abstract is the 950-node column; the text of Section 4.2 gives 400 virtual nodes as the operating point. The abstract does not state the node count.

assertions.value: The authors report using the AudioMNIST database (30,000 spoken digit samples, 60 speakers, 48 kHz), down-sampled to 12 kHz with librosa and zero-padded to a total sample size of 12, 000, then converted to a cochleagram with a Lyon cochlear model.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.3, Isolate spoken digit recognition, p.7
quotes: contain 30,000 spoken digits(0-9) audio samples of 60 diﬀerent speakers with a sampling rate of 48 kHz
down-sample the audio to 12 kHz using the librosa package [49]
to make total sample size of 12, 000
Lyons cochlear ear model to get the cochleagram
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.3 states the data and preprocessing.

assertions.value: The authors report using the first 5 speakers to form 20 balanced subsets of 100 audio samples (5 speakers x 10 digits x 2 utterances), training on the first 4 of 5 subsets and testing on the last, and forming 50 datasets from random combinations of 5 of the 20 subsets to measure word error rate (WER).
assertions.anchor: Section 4.3, Isolate spoken digit recognition, p.7
quotes: we consider ﬁrst 5 speakers from the AudioMNIST database to create 20 balanced subset
each containing 5 speaker × 10 digit × 2 utterance each, i.e. 100 audio sample
with the ﬁrst 4 used for training and the last one for testing
50 datasets are formed using random combinations of 5 subsets from 20 subsets
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.3 states the evaluation protocol.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 lists this paper's training/testing size as 475/25 digits repeated 20 times, which does not match the 400/100 split and 50 datasets in Section 4.3.

assertions.value: The authors state the input mask is a real valued matrix with uniform distribution in [-1,1], the cochleagram has 77 frequency channels, the product of mask and cochleagram is injected serially, and the output class is the maximum argument of the row-wise mean of the estimation matrix.
quotes: real valued matrix of dimension
with uniform distribution in [-1,1]
Output class is predicted by getting the maximum argument corresponding to row-wise mean of estimation matrix.
Frequency Channel=77
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4.3 and Fig. 6 give the mask and readout.

assertions.value: The authors report a testing word error rate for isolated spoken digit recognition of 0.34% mean with a standard deviation of 0.51% (Table 3),; Table 3 also lists a lower training WER.
quotes: Table 3. WER for Isolated spoken digit recognition task for training and testing phase.
a WER ∼ 0.34% for the speech recognition
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experimental system.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 lists reference 31 at WER=0.04%, lower than this paper's 0.34%, so the system is not the best on this task in the paper's own table.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their system tops the prediction accuracy in the first two tests (NARMA-10 and Santa Fe) and is the only reported system to perform well in all three tasks, comparing against the systems of its comparison table.
quotes: the present RC system tops the prediction accuracy in the ﬁrst two test, and is the only reported system to perform well in all three tasks
assertions.certainty_reason: Author claim from a comparison table of works with differing protocols.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 mixes metrics (NMSE for most references, NRMSE for this paper on NARMA10), sample sizes and sampling rates, so the ranking is not like for like.

assertions.value: The authors list in their comparison table prior opto-electronic systems on NARMA10: NMSE 0.230 +/- 0.023, NMSE 0.181 +/- 0.013, NRMSE 0.185, and NMSE 0.168 +/- 0.015, against NRMSE 0.142 +/- 6.5 x 10^-3 for this paper.
quotes: NRMSE=0.185
assertions.certainty_reason: Values attributed to other works.
assertions.reader_inference: NMSE is the square of NRMSE, so NMSE values and NRMSE values in this table are not directly comparable.

assertions.value: The authors list in their comparison table prior results: Santa Fe NMSE 0.124 +/- 4 x 10^-4; spoken digit WER 0.04% +/- 0.017% and 0.6% +/- 0.2%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values attributed to other works.

assertions.value: The authors state that the system currently works at a low speed, mostly limited by the sampling rate of the ADC and the settling time of the DAC, and expect a significant speedup from a faster ADC and DAC.
quotes: Our system is currently working at a low speed, which is mostly limited by the sampling rate of ADC and settling time of DAC.
A signiﬁcant speedup is expected by choosing a faster ADC and DAC.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 states this limit.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup is a projection; no faster ADC or DAC is tested.

assertions.value: The authors claim the bulk-optical EOM could be replaced by photonic integrated chips, that the design is easily reconfigurable for more neurons, higher connectivity and arbitrary topology, and that performance and robustness could be further improved by online training; none of these is tested in the paper.
quotes: it is prospective to replace the existing bulk-optical EOM with photonic integrated chips
easily re-conﬁgurable to accommodate even more neurons, high connectivity, and arbitrary topology
the performance and robustness of the present RC could be further improved by online training
assertions.certainty_reason: Forward-looking author claims.
assertions.reader_inference: The Conclusions also say the system allows online training, but Section 3 sends state data to a PC and Section 4 does not describe online training.

assertions.value: The authors claim the system could find applications in real-time information processing, weather forecasting and financial analysis; no such application is tested.
quotes: could ﬁnd a wealth of impactful applications in real-time information processing, weather forecasting, and ﬁnancial analysis
assertions.certainty_reason: Author claim without evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state the system is characterized by three benchmark tasks: NARMA-10, Santa Fe laser data prediction and isolate spoken digit recognition, and they claim the results show robustness and versatility.
quotes: To characterize the system, we run three benchmark tasks
All exhibit exceptionally high performance, which indicates the robustness and versatility of this RC system.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 states the evaluation scope.
